A · From Time to Frequency Key Terms — The DFT

DFT

/ˌdiː.efˈtiː/ · Discrete Fourier Transform — "FOOR-ee-ay"

Takes N samples in and returns how much of each frequency is inside.

การแปลงฟูริเยร์แบบไม่ต่อเนื่อง — เปลี่ยนสัญญาณจากมุมเวลาเป็นมุมความถี่

Spectrum

/ˈspek.trəm/

The list the DFT hands back — one number per frequency, drawn as bars.

สเปกตรัม — ลิสต์ที่ DFT คืนมา · หนึ่งตัวเลขต่อหนึ่งความถี่ วาดเป็นแท่ง

Frequency bin

/ˈfriː.kwən.si bɪn/

One slot in the DFT output. Each slot stands for one specific frequency.

ช่องความถี่หนึ่งช่องในผลลัพธ์ DFT · หนึ่งช่อง = หนึ่งความถี่

Magnitude

/ˈmæɡ.nɪ.tʃuːd/

How much of that frequency is present — the height of the bar, written |X[k]|.

ความแรงของความถี่นั้น — ความสูงของแท่ง เขียนว่า |X[k]|

Probe e−j2πkn/N

/prəʊb/ · textbooks call it the basis function

The reference sinusoid the DFT holds against your signal — one per frequency. Multiply, add up: that is the score.

คลื่นรูปไซน์อ้างอิงที่ DFT ยกขึ้นมาเทียบกับสัญญาณ — หนึ่งตัวต่อหนึ่งความถี่ · คูณ sample กับมันแล้วบวกรวม จะได้คะแนนของความถี่นั้น

🔑

A DFT turns a list of samples into a list of frequencies — the rest is reading that list.

↔️

Session 5: three sinusoids in → one complicated wave out. This session: one complicated wave in → the three sinusoids out. Nothing is added and nothing is lost — it is the same signal, described the other way round.

1 / 59
A · From Time to Frequency How it un-mixes: one probe frequency at a time
🔍

The DFT holds up a reference sinusoid, asks "how much of you is in here?", writes down the answer, and moves to the next frequency. A spectrum is just that list of answers, drawn as bars.

1 / 59
A · From Time to Frequency The DFT, step by step — where one bar comes from

① pick a frequency to ask about

② multiply the signal by that probe

③ add every product up

④ that total is one bar

⑤ repeat for every frequency

💡

These five steps are the whole DFT. A matching probe rides in step with the signal, so the products stay above zero and the total grows; a probe that does not match cancels itself out. Nothing decides which frequencies are "in there" — the cancelling does. And a bar is not a new idea: one bar = one total.

1 / 59
A · From Time to Frequency The DFT formula says exactly that
X[k]=∑n=0N−1​x[n]e−j2πkn/N

x[n]

your samples — the recording you already have

k

which probe frequency we are asking about right now

e−j2πkn/N

the probe itself — Euler's formula from Session 5

∑

multiply sample by probe, add it all up — that is the score

😌

You will not be computing this sum by hand in your work — np.fft.rfft(x) does it in one line. Recognising the formula matters; grinding it does not. We open it up once in sub-topic D so it is not a black box.

1 / 59
A · From Time to Frequency 🌍 Why bother: some things only exist in the frequency view
⚡

Mains hum — the 50 Hz buzz you hear from an unshielded guitar lead. Every mains cable radiates a field swinging 50 times a second, and any nearby wire or electrode picks it up without touching it: ECG (electrocardiogram — the heart's electrical signal), microphones, lab instruments. 60 Hz in the Americas and Japan. You cannot remove what you cannot locate; the DFT is what locates it.

A · From Time to Frequency ↩ Back to the opening question
Q

How does it know how much bass is in the sound?

A

It runs a DFT on a short slice of the sound, then groups the bins into bands and draws one bar per band.

🎚️

Turning up "bass" on an equalizer means scaling the low-frequency bins — an idea we will come back to when we build filters in Session 8.

A · From Time to Frequency
💻 LAB — Your first spectrum, in five lines
①Build a signal with two tones you chose yourself
②Transform it
③Plot the magnitude against hertz
lab_a.pyColab · no downloads needed
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fs, N = 1000, 1000                      # 1000 samples/s, 1 second
t = np.arange(N)/fs
x = np.cos(2*np.pi*50*t) + 0.6*np.cos(2*np.pi*120*t)
mag  = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2/N       # magnitude, scaled back to amplitude
freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)             # the hertz each bin stands for
plt.plot(freq, mag); plt.xlim(0, 300); plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.show()
✅

You should see exactly two spikes, at 50 Hz with height ≈ 1.0 and at 120 Hz with height ≈ 0.6 — the two numbers you typed in, read back out of the sum.

A · From Time to Frequency 🔍 Explore — does the bar really track the amplitude?

Keep everything fixed, change only how loud the 120 Hz tone is:

explore_a.py
for a in [0.0, 0.25, 0.6, 1.0]:
    x = np.cos(2*np.pi*50*t) + a*np.cos(2*np.pi*120*t)
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2/N
    print("a =", a,
          "| bar at  50 Hz =", round(mag[50], 2),
          "| bar at 120 Hz =", round(mag[120], 2))
🔎

The 120 Hz bar prints 0.0, 0.25, 0.6, 1.0 while the 50 Hz bar never moves. Each frequency is measured independently of the others — that is why one loud tone cannot hide a quiet one at a different frequency. Now try a = 0.6 with the frequency changed to 121 Hz and watch the tidy spike get untidy; sub-topic C explains why.

B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum Key Terms — Spectrum Reading

Peak

/piːk/

A tall, narrow spike — one frequency that is strongly present.

ยอดแหลม = ความถี่ที่เด่นในสัญญาณ

DC component

/ˌdiːˈsiː/ · Direct Current

Bin 0 — the average value of the signal. A big bin 0 means the signal is not centred on zero.

ช่อง 0 = ค่าเฉลี่ยของสัญญาณ (ความถี่ศูนย์)

Harmonic

/hɑːˈmɒn.ɪk/

One note, several peaks. Play A4 and the instrument adds 880 and 1320 on top of 440 by itself. Evenly spaced peaks = one note, not many.

ฮาร์มอนิก — โน้ตเดียวแต่ได้หลายยอด · ดีด A4 แล้วเครื่องดนตรีเติม 880 กับ 1320 ให้เอง · ยอดเรียงห่างเท่ากัน = โน้ตเดียว

Noise floor

/nɔɪz flɔːr/

The low, bumpy carpet the peaks stand on. A peak counts only if it clears the floor.

พื้นสัญญาณรบกวน — ระดับพื้นที่ยอดต้องโผล่พ้นจึงจะนับ

🔑

Four words are enough to describe almost any spectrum out loud: "one peak here, harmonics above it, a floor at this level, and a DC term."

1 / 59
B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum Two axes, two questions
📐

Horizontal = which frequency. Vertical = how much of it. That is the entire reading instruction. Everything harder comes from signals with more than one thing in them.

1 / 59
B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum Four shapes you will meet again and again
👂

One spike = a pure tone · two spikes = two things at once · evenly spaced spikes = one note with its harmonics, which is what makes an instrument sound like itself · no spike at all = noise, energy everywhere and nowhere.

1 / 59
B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum Half of the output is a reflection — read the left half
🪞

For anything you recorded, two peaks that add up to fs​ are one tone counted twice — 120 + 880 = 1000. So read 0 to fs​/2 always, not only when you spot the twin; np.fft.rfft does it for you. (N = 1000 samples in, k = the slot number, so bin 120's twin is bin N−k = 880. Complex I/Q data from a radio is the one exception.) Not the same thing as aliasing (Session 2): the mirror is always there and costs you nothing, while aliasing means something above fs​/2 got in and is now lying to you about where it sits.

x[n] = 1.00·cos(2π·3n/32)

B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum 🌍 Use case: the tuner in your phone
1

Record a fraction of a second and transform it.

2

Find the lowest strong peak — that is the note being played, not the tallest one.

3

Compare it with the nearest note in a standard table (A4 = 440 Hz) and show the gap.

🎻

A violin and a flute playing the same A4 share the peak at 440 Hz. What differs is how tall the harmonics above it are — that pattern is what your ear calls "tone colour".

1 / 59
B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum ↩ Flute or drum? You can answer now

Evenly spaced spikes

A pitched instrument. The lowest spike is the note (440 Hz = A4); the ones above it are harmonics at 2×, 3×, 4×.

→ this one is the flute.

Energy smeared everywhere

No repeating pattern to lock onto, just a bulge low down where the skin resonates.

→ this one is the drum.

🎯

This is the whole skill in one sentence: you are reading a pattern, not a single number. A tuner needs one peak; telling a flute from a drum needs the shape.

B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum
💻 LAB — Read a real recording: where is the heartbeat?
①Load 10 seconds of a real ECG
②Transform it
③Search only the band a heart rate can live in
lab_b.pyfirst run downloads ~1 MB — needs internet
from scipy.datasets import electrocardiogram
x  = electrocardiogram()[:3600]              # 10 s of MIT-BIH record 208
fs, N = 360, len(x)
mag  = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x - x.mean())) * 2/N   # remove DC before transforming
freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)
plt.plot(freq, mag); plt.xlim(0, 10); plt.xlabel("Hz"); plt.show()
band = (freq > 0.7) & (freq < 3.0)                 # a plausible heart rate
print(freq[band][mag[band].argmax()]*60, "beats per minute")
⚠️

Prints 60.0 beats per minute — but the tallest peak on the plot is not the heartbeat, it is baseline drift below 0.5 Hz (the patient breathing). That is why the code searches a band instead of calling argmax on everything. The tallest peak is not automatically your answer.

B · Reading a Magnitude Spectrum 🔍 Explore — how much noise can a peak survive?
explore_b.py
for nz in [0.3, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]:
    rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
    x = (np.cos(2*np.pi*120*t) + 0.6*np.cos(2*np.pi*300*t)
         + nz*rng.normal(size=N))
    mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2/N
    floor = np.median(mag)
    print(nz, "peak", round(mag[120], 2),
              "floor", round(floor, 3),
              "ratio", round(mag[120]/floor, 1))
🔎

The peak height barely moves — 0.99, 0.98, 0.97, 0.91 — while the floor climbs from 0.015 to 0.25 and the peak-to-floor ratio collapses from 67 to under 4. A tone concentrates its energy into one bin; noise spreads the same energy over all of them. That is why the frequency view can find a tone you cannot hear.

🌍 In the real world

A DFT divides frequency into equal slots in exactly the same way. A 2000 Hz tone — which slot does it land in?

C · Frequency Bins Key Terms — Bins

Bin index (k)

/bɪn ˈɪn.deks/

The position of a slot in the output: 0, 1, 2, … N−1. Just a counter, not a frequency.

เลขช่องในผลลัพธ์ DFT (0 ถึง N−1) — เป็นแค่ลำดับ ยังไม่ใช่ความถี่

Bin spacing (Δf)

/ˈdel.tə ef/ — "delta f"

The gap in hertz between neighbouring slots: Δf=fs​/N.

ระยะห่างระหว่างช่อง (เฮิรตซ์) = fs​/N

Bin frequency

/bɪn ˈfriː.kwən.si/

The hertz a slot stands for: fk​=kfs​/N.

ความถี่จริงของช่อง k = kfs​/N

Nyquist bin

"NIGH-kwist" /ˈnaɪ.kwɪst/

Bin N/2, sitting at fs​/2 — the highest frequency the samples can describe (Session 2).

ช่องกลาง (N/2) ที่ fs​/2 — ความถี่สูงสุดที่ข้อมูลอธิบายได้

📣

Never report a bin number to anyone outside this room. The bin number is k (which slot, counting from 0), and "bin 25" means nothing without fs​ (the sample rate) and N (how many samples went in). "250 Hz" means the same thing to everybody.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins N samples in → N slots out, evenly spaced to fs​
📏

N does two jobs: how many samples you transformed, and how many slots come back. Not the whole recording — just the block you handed over. The slots are evenly spaced from zero. Bin k sits at fk​=kfs​/N — bin 0 is the average (DC), and each step up is one more Δf. That list of bins, each with its own height, is the spectrum — the bars you have been reading since sub-topic B are one per bin.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins Record longer to tell two close tones apart
🔬

Two close tones fade in and out against each other, and that fade is the only sign there are two of them. Stop recording before the first fade and no transform can help you — the evidence is not in the clip. (Δf=fs​/N says it in arithmetic: more samples, finer slots.)

So: to separate two frequencies, record for longer — nothing else works.

But: a long window cannot say when anything happened. That trade is all of Session 7.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins Going the other way — and what happens between slots
k=fN/fs​

f = the frequency you are asking about (Hz) · k = the slot it lands in · N = samples you transformed · fs​ = sample rate

Same relationship, rearranged. "Which slot does 2000 Hz fall in?" is a division, not a new formula.

❌

Common mistake: assuming every tone lands neatly on a slot. It only does when f is a whole multiple of Δf. Otherwise the energy spills into the neighbours — this is called spectral leakage.

💡

Leakage is not a bug and it does not hide the tone — it smears it. You still read "about 105 Hz" from the picture; you just cannot claim four-digit precision from a 10 Hz ruler.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins Taper the ends — fade them to zero, and the spill goes away

The DFT reads your clip as if it looped forever, so a tone that does not fit a whole number of times leaves a step at the join — and the spill you saw on the last two slides is the DFT describing that step. To taper is simply to fade the start and the end down to zero, so the loop joins smoothly.

You gain (lower panel, a tone that does not fit): the spill collapses — 14 slots → 4.

You pay (upper panel, a tone that fits exactly): it used to sit in 1 slot → now 3 — close tones get harder to separate.

🪟

One line of code: np.fft.rfft(x * np.hanning(len(x))) — and divide by w.sum()/2 instead of N/2 to keep amplitudes readable. Hann is the safe default; the others (Hamming, Blackman, flat-top) trade the same two things in different ratios.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins 🌍 Use case: everyone divides frequency into slots
📻

Radio, Wi-Fi and mobile networks all carve the spectrum into numbered slots — same idea as bins, agreed in advance so devices can talk about them.

🔧

Condition monitoring on a factory floor lives on this conversion: a maintenance engineer needs hertz, because that is what matches a shaft speed or a bearing specification.

🗣️

Converting bin → hertz is the moment your analysis becomes something another person can act on.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins ↩ So which slot does 2000 Hz land in?
Givenfs = 8000 Hz, N = 8
SpacingΔf = 8000 / 8 = 1000 Hz
Slotk = 2000 / 1000 = 2
∴ a 2000 Hz tone lands in bin 2

Remember one thing and you never need two formulas: one step up the ruler is fs​/N hertz. Everything else is multiplying or dividing by it.

1 / 59
C · Frequency Bins
💻 LAB — Let the library do the bin arithmetic
①Transform a 2000 Hz tone
②Find the loudest bin
③Check the library against the formula
lab_c.pyColab · no downloads needed
fs, N = 8000, 800                      # 0.1 s at 8 kHz
t = np.arange(N)/fs
x = np.cos(2*np.pi*2000*t)
mag  = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2/N
freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)        # the library's bin -> Hz table
k = mag.argmax()
print("bin spacing", fs/N, "Hz")
print("peak bin", k, "-> library says", freq[k], "Hz")
print("by hand: k*fs/N =", k*fs/N, "Hz")
✅

Prints spacing 10.0 Hz · peak bin 200 · 2000.0 Hz both ways. rfftfreq is just kfs​/N evaluated for every k — and now you can check it.

C · Frequency Bins 🔍 Explore — buy resolution with recording time

Two tones 2 Hz apart. Keep fs​ fixed and record for longer and longer:

explore_c.pyis there an empty slot between the two tones?
fs = 64
for N in [16, 32, 64, 128]:
    tt   = np.arange(N)/fs
    x    = np.cos(2*np.pi*10*tt) + np.cos(2*np.pi*12*tt)
    m    = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(x)) * 2/N
    freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(N, 1/fs)
    gap  = m[(freq > 10) & (freq < 12)]   # slots between the tones
    ok   = len(gap) and gap.min() < 0.5
    print(N, round(fs/N, 2), "Hz", "separated" if ok else "one lump")
🔎

N = 16 and 32 → "one lump" (slots 4 and 2 Hz apart, nothing fits between the tones); N = 64 and 128 → "separated" (slots 1 and 0.5 Hz apart, so at least one empty slot sits between them). Resolution means there is a gap, not just two tall bars. Rule of thumb: Δf under half the separation — the tones are 2 Hz apart, so you need 1 Hz slots, which is one full second of recording. Doubling fs​ instead makes it worse: same N, wider slots.

D · Inside the DFT Key Terms — What the Box Contains

Probe value

also called a twiddle factor /ˈtwɪd.əl/

One value of e−j2πkn/N — the number a sample gets multiplied by. For N = 4 there are only four of them.

ค่าตัวคูณจาก Euler ที่ใช้กับแต่ละ sample · N = 4 มีแค่ 4 ค่า

Complex output

/ˈkɒm.pleks/ · written a+jb

Each bin comes out as two numbers at once: how much, and where in its cycle it starts.

ผลลัพธ์แต่ละช่องเป็นจำนวนเชิงซ้อน (มีสองส่วน)

Magnitude ∣X[k]∣

/ˈmæɡ.nɪ.tʃuːd/

a2+b2​ — the single number that gets plotted. Everything you read in sub-topic B was this.

√(a²+b²) — ค่าที่เอาไปพล็อตเป็นความสูงของแท่ง

DC term X[0]

/ˌdiːˈsiː tɜːm/

Bin 0, where every probe value equals 1 — so it is simply the sum of all the samples.

ช่อง 0 · ตัวคูณเป็น 1 ทั้งหมด จึงเป็นผลบวกของ sample ทุกตัว

🧩

Nothing here is new. The probe values come from Euler's formula in Session 5, and magnitude from a right-angled triangle.

1 / 59
D · Inside the DFT For N = 4 the whole alphabet is four values

For bin k=1 of a 4-point DFT (that is N=4 — four samples in, four bins out), the probe e−j2πn/4 takes one quarter turn around the circle per sample:

n = 0 →  1
n = 1 → −j
n = 2 → −1
n = 3 →  j
🔁

Then it repeats — there is no fifth value. Any N cuts the circle into N equal steps of 360/N degrees; bin k jumps k steps per sample. N=10 would be ten points 36° apart — same idea, but only N=4 is tidy enough to do on paper.

D · Inside the DFT So the transform is: multiply, then add
the four samples: x = [1, 0, −1, 0] for n=0,1,2,3
slide 9's formula: X[k]=∑n=0N−1​x[n]e−j2πkn/N
1 Fix the bin
set k=1, N=4 X[1]=∑n=03​x[n]e−j2πn/4
2 Write the sum out
one term per sample =x[0]e−j0+x[1]e−jπ/2+x[2]e−jπ+x[3]e−j3π/2
3 Put in the probes
the four values from slide 39 =x[0](1)+x[1](−j)+x[2](−1)+x[3](j)
4 Put in the samples
from the strip above =(1)(1)+(0)(−j)+(−1)(−1)+(0)(j)
5 Multiply, then add
the two zeros drop out =1+0+1+0=2
🎯

Bin 0 is the same five steps with k=0, where every probe is 1, so X[0]=1+0+(−1)+0=0: this signal is already centred on zero, no DC offset. There is no third operation inside the box — a DFT of a million points is this, a million times over. The full four-bin trace is in 🧮 Practice & Review.

1 / 59
D · Inside the DFT The output is two numbers; the plot shows one
∣X[k]∣=a2+b2​

The previous slide handed you a bin; this turns it into a bar. Every bin is X[k]=a+jb, where b is the number in front of j. So X[1]=1−j gives ∣X[1]∣=12+(−1)2​≈1.41, the height that gets drawn.

❌

Two traps: dropping the minus before squaring — a magnitude is never negative. And putting a number in for j: j never gets a value.

🕐

What we drop is the phase — where that frequency starts. Filters need it (Session 8).

1 / 59
D · Inside the DFT 🌍 Why nobody runs the DFT the way we just did
⚡

Every bin needs N multiply-and-adds, and there are N bins — so the direct recipe costs about N2. The FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) reorganises the same arithmetic to cost about Nlog2​N: for one second of CD audio (N = 44,100) that is the difference between two billion operations and about 700 thousand. Same answer, ~100× to ~3000× less work. That is Session 7.

💻 LAB — Check the box against your own arithmetic
①Transform the same four samples
②Look at the complex output
③Take the magnitude and compare with the bars
lab_d.pyColab · no downloads needed
x = np.array([1, 0, -1, 0])
X = np.fft.fft(x)
print("complex :", np.round(X, 3))
print("magnitude:", np.abs(X))
print("probe values for k=1:",
      np.round(np.exp(-2j*np.pi*1*np.arange(4)/4), 2))
✅

Prints [0.+0.j 2.+0.j 0.+0.j 2.+0.j], magnitudes [0. 2. 0. 2.], and probe values [1.+0.j 0.-1.j -1.-0.j -0.+1.j] — the 1, −j, −1, j from the circle, and the 2 you worked out by hand. The box is now open.

D · Inside the DFT 🔍 Explore — what survives when you slide the signal along?

Same four samples, started at a different place each time:

explore_d.py
for s in range(4):
    X = np.fft.fft(np.roll(x, s))
    print("shift", s,
          "| magnitude", np.abs(X).round(2),
          "| phase", np.angle(X, deg=True).round(0))
🔎

The magnitude line never changes — [0. 2. 0. 2.] every time — while the phase at bin 1 steps through 0°, −90°, 180°, 90° — a quarter turn per shift, wrapped into the ±180° range. Magnitude answers "which frequencies"; phase answers "starting where". This is also the honest reason a magnitude spectrum cannot tell you when something happened — the problem that Session 7's spectrogram exists to solve.

D · Inside the DFT 🎯 Your Turn — predict first, then run
🎯

Before you touch the keyboard: for y = [2, 0, 2, 0], which bins will be non-zero? Write your answer down. Hint: bin 0 is the sum, and this signal repeats every 2 samples.

your_turn_d.pyfill in the TODOs
y = np.array([2, 0, 2, 0])
# TODO 1: write your prediction as a comment before running anything
# TODO 2: compute X[0] by hand (it is just the sum) and check it
# TODO 3: run np.fft.fft(y) and compare the magnitudes with your prediction
# TODO 4: in one sentence — why does bin 2 hold energy for this signal?
✅

Expected: X = [4, 0, 4, 0]. Bin 0 = 2+0+2+0 = 4 (the average is not zero this time). Bin 2 is the fastest frequency a 4-point DFT can describe — one full flip every two samples — and [2,0,2,0] does exactly that, so all the rest of the energy lands there. Reading which bin lights up, and why, is the skill that carries into Session 7.

Where you can use this 🌍 Same question, three different worlds

Every one of these reduces to "which frequency is strong, and should it be there?"

🎵

Music & audio

The problem: which note is playing, and on what instrument?

What the spectrum gives: the lowest peak names the note; the harmonic pattern names the instrument.

tuners · automatic transcription · equalizers · karaoke pitch scoring

🫀

Medicine

The problem: a recording of the body is buried in interference.

What the spectrum gives: the mains hum sits at 50 Hz, the heart rhythm around 1 Hz, muscle noise higher up — separable because they live at different frequencies.

ECG · EEG (brain activity) · heart-sound screening · sleep staging

🐦

Environment

The problem: what is out there, and how loud is it?

What the spectrum gives: each species calls in its own band, so a microphone in a forest becomes a census.

bird-call identification · urban noise mapping · engine-noise compliance

1 / 59
Where you can use this 🌍 And three where nobody is listening to anything

⚙️ Machines

A peak that was not there last month is a bearing beginning to fail. Condition monitoring is comparing this month's spectrum with last month's.

📡 Communications

Every channel is a band and interference is an overlap. The spectrum is how you see who is stepping on whom.

📈 Data over time

Sales, traffic, server load, footfall. A peak at one cycle per seven days is a weekly rhythm you can plan staffing around.

🔁

Note what changed and what did not: the sampling rate here is one sample per day, so the axis reads in cycles per day instead of hertz. The formula is untouched — fk​=kfs​/N does not care what the units are.

Where you can use this 🌍 Turning a domain into your own project
a good topic = a signal you can record yourself + a frequency question you cannot answer by eye

"Does my fan sound different when it is dirty?"

Record before and after cleaning · compare the two spectra · report which peaks moved.

"Which room in the house is noisiest, and at what frequency?"

Same 10-second recording in five rooms · one spectrum each · rank them.

"Does the campus shuttle really run on a cycle?"

Count arrivals per 10 minutes for a week · transform the counts · read the period.

📥

Where to get data: your own phone microphone (a free recorder app exports WAV) · open ECG and machine-fault datasets · open city sensor portals · your own logs and counts.

⚠️

Sanity-check before you commit: is the thing you care about periodic? The DFT finds repetition. A one-off bang or a slow drift is a job for a different tool.

🧮Worked Example — Reading a Spectrum
Lookpeaks at 220, 440, 660, 880 Hz
Spacing440−220 = 220 · 660−440 = 220
Patternwhole multiples of 220 → harmonics
Name itlowest peak = the note = A3
∴ one note at 220 Hz, not four separate tones
❌

Reporting "four tones present". Evenly spaced peaks that are whole multiples of the lowest are one source.

✎Quick Check — What Made This Spectrum?⏱ 2 min

A one-second recording gives a spectrum with a single tall spike at 300 Hz, a flat carpet at 0.02, and nothing else. What was recorded — and what would the same signal look like in the time view?

✅

A single pure tone at 300 Hz, with very little noise. No harmonics means nothing musical or mechanical with a body to it — an electronic beep, a test tone, or a single-frequency interference. In the time view it is a plain repeating cosine, one cycle every 1/300 s ≈ 3.3 ms.

1 / 59
🧮Worked Example — Bin ↔ Hertz, Both Directions

Given

  • CD-quality audio, fs​ = 44,100 Hz
  • we transform N = 4,410 samples (0.1 s)

Find

  • (a) what frequency is bin 30?
  • (b) which bin does a 1000 Hz tone land in?
Step 1Δf = fs/N = 44100/4410 = 10 Hz
(a)f = k·Δf = 30 × 10 = 300 Hz
(b)k = f/Δf = 1000/10 = bin 100
∴ bin 30 = 300 Hz · 1000 Hz = bin 100
🔑

One quantity does both jobs: Δf=fs​/N. Multiply by it to go bin → hertz, divide by it to go back.

1 / 59
✎Quick Check — A Sensor Reading⏱ 3 min

A vibration sensor samples at fs​ = 2000 Hz and you transform N = 200 samples. A strong peak sits at bin 25. (a) What frequency is the machine vibrating at? (b) If you recorded 400 samples instead, what would change?

✅

(a) Δf = 2000/200 = 10 Hz, so the peak is at 25 × 10 = 250 Hz.  (b) Doubling N at the same fs​ halves the spacing to 5 Hz — the recording lasts 0.2 s instead of 0.1 s, and the same tone would now appear at bin 50. Finer ruler, same tone.

1 / 59
🧮Worked Example — A Four-Point DFT, End to End
X[0]1 + 0 + (−1) + 0 = 0
X[1]1(1) + 0(−j) + (−1)(−1) + 0(j) = 2
X[2]1(1) + 0(−1) + (−1)(1) + 0(−1) = 0
X[3]1(1) + 0(j) + (−1)(−1) + 0(−j) = 2
∴ X = [0, 2, 0, 2]

Every value came out real here, so the magnitudes are the same four numbers. Bins 1 and 3 are the mirror pair — one tone, reported twice, exactly as sub-topic B promised.

📋The Case — A Pump That Sounds Different

Maintenance recorded pump 4B and sent you the spectrum. Last month it had only the tall peak; this month there is a second one.

Answer these

  • Q1 — convert both peaks to hertz
  • Q2 — which one is the pump simply running, and which is the newcomer worth investigating?
  • Q3 — a colleague suspects there are really two tones close together inside the tall peak. What would you change about the recording to find out?
✔Part A — Answers
Q1Δf = 4000/400 = 10 Hz → bin 10 = 100 Hz, bin 47 = 470 Hz
Q2100 Hz is the running speed — tall, steady, there last month.
470 Hz is the newcomer, and it is not a whole multiple of 100 Hz,
so it is not a harmonic of the shaft — something else is vibrating.
Q3Record longer at the same fs. 4000 samples (1 s) gives Δf = 1 Hz,
enough to split tones a few hertz apart. Raising fs would make it worse.
🧠

Q2 is the part that needs a human. The transform can tell you 470 Hz; deciding that 470 Hz is suspicious takes knowing what the machine is supposed to do — which is exactly why DSP is a tool for domain experts, not a replacement for them.

💻Q4 — The Same Three Steps, In Code
case.pyfill in the TODOs
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
fs, N = 4000, 400
tt  = np.arange(N)/fs
pump = (np.sin(2*np.pi*100*tt) + 0.45*np.sin(2*np.pi*470*tt)
        + 0.10*rng.normal(size=N))
# TODO 1: transform  ->  mag = np.abs(np.fft.rfft(pump)) * 2/N
# TODO 2: find every bin whose magnitude clears 10x the median floor
# TODO 3: print each of those bins in Hz, using k*fs/N
# TODO 4: rerun with N = 4000 (1 second) and print the new bin spacing
✅

Expected: the floor sits near 0.007, so a 10× threshold keeps exactly two bins — 10 → 100.0 Hz (0.99) and 47 → 470.0 Hz (0.45). With N = 4000 the spacing drops to 1 Hz. Transform, threshold against the floor, convert to hertz — the same three steps on your own project data.
